_comment: Issue #88 (B5.2). The compliance half of the release record: who owns the
copyright, under which licence the work is distributed, which links a store
reviewer is given, which artifacts each distribution target actually ships,
and which performance numbers travel with the release.
It is a sibling of container/release-manifest.json rather than part of it, and
the split is along one line: the manifest records what a Docker build produced
and nothing else. Adding a field to it that a build does not produce needs
either a two-architecture rebuild to change one string, or a no-build write
path into the file that carries the build record - and the second is a hole in
exactly the guard #174 put there. So everything derivable from the repository
without building lives here and in provenance/, and the bundle is
tied to the manifest by the manifest's own SHA-256 so the two cannot drift
Nothing in this file is hand-maintained arithmetic. provenance/ is
regenerated by `go run ./cmd/provenance -write` from apps/common, and the
checks in provenance_test.go and compliance_test.go re-derive every hash and
every component list from the tree on each run.

copyrightNote: A collective authorship line rather than a named person or company. §6 pins
the display name and app id; it names no legal entity, and inventing one in
a licence header is not this issue's call to make.

rationale: Every component that reaches a shipped artifact is permissive (MIT,
BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, Apache-2.0 or CC0-1.0) except the two named
below. That set is the Go modules `go list -deps` reports as linked into
either binary on either shipped architecture, plus the production packages
in ui/shared's lockfile, and third-party-licenses.json is re-derived from
both on every run. The tally lives there and is not repeated here: this
file used to carry a module count that had been stale for a long time,
and a number in prose is a claim nothing checks, so
TestTheProseCarriesNoCountNobodyChecks refuses one. rclone itself, the one
dependency this product is built around, is MIT.
Two components are NOT permissive, and this file used to say the graph had
no copyleft in it. That stopped being true when rclone's s3 backend was
registered (#235), and the sentence is deleted rather than softened.
github.com/hashicorp/go-cleanhttp@v0.5.2 and
github.com/hashicorp/go-retryablehttp@v0.7.8 are both MPL-2.0. They arrive
under backend/s3 through github.com/IBM/go-sdk-core/v5, which
backend/s3's ibm_signer.go imports with no build tag, so registering the
backend and not linking them is not a choice this project has.
They are in the binaries and not merely in go.mod, which is a difference
worth measuring rather than asserting: `go tool nm` on a linux/amd64
backup-manager finds 17 go-retryablehttp symbols and 1 go-cleanhttp symbol
surviving dead-code elimination, among them the code symbols NewClient,
DefaultRetryPolicy, DefaultBackoff and DefaultPooledTransport. The MPL
code ships and runs, and nothing below should be read as suggesting it
does not.
Shipping it is a decision and it was taken on purpose. MPL-2.0 is
FILE-level weak copyleft: it scopes reciprocity to the covered files, and
§3.3 permits distributing a Larger Work under other terms, so Apache-2.0
over the whole is not foreclosed. The two alternatives both cost more than
they buy. Dropping the s3 backend removes the only non-local storage medium
the product has. Forking rclone to delete ibm_signer.go is a cost on every
upgrade, and docs/rclone-upgrade.md exists to keep that surface at zero.
§3.3's permission is conditional, and the condition is the whole cost:
a Larger Work may ship under terms of this project's choice PROVIDED it
also complies with the MPL for the covered software. So Apache-2.0 here
rests on §3.2 being met, not merely on §3.3 existing.
§3.2(a) asks two things, and they are worth keeping apart because they
land differently. The source has to be made available: it is, at the
immutable Go module proxy address recorded in acceptedNonPermissive
below, per RELEASE rather than per licence, at no charge, without an
account, and independently of this
repository being private. Neither module is modified or vendored, so that
address serves the same bytes that were compiled and go.sum pins them. And
recipients OF THE EXECUTABLE FORM have to be informed how to obtain it:
NOTICE and docs/compliance/source-offer.md do that, naming each module at
its exact version with its own address, and the gate reads both and fails
if either stops. NOTICE also travels with what this project distributes:
the runtime image carries it at /licenses/NOTICE beside /licenses/LICENSE,
and TestTheImageCarriesTheLicenceAndTheNotice reads the runtime stage and
fails if either COPY goes. Until it did, the image copied the binaries and
the frontend bundle and nothing else, a gap that predates this decision
and cost Apache-2.0 §4(d) the same way; the rest of it, the inventory
inside the image and a per-target rule, is #407's.
acceptedNonPermissive is a third category rather than two more entries on
permissiveIds, and that is not bookkeeping. permissiveIds says what a
licence IS and it is the list a reviewer reads to find out whether this
graph is permissive. Widening it would have cleared the check in one line
by making this file assert something false about the two components it is
least true of. An entry in acceptedNonPermissive cannot be a bare id: it
has to name the clause, the licence text address, a per-release source
address and the exact releases it covers, and
LicenceObligationComplaints reads the artifacts it claims and
fails the build when they do not carry the offer. So the acceptance is
checked the same way the permissive claim is, and turning it into a
formality takes deleting a test rather than editing a list.
Apache-2.0 over MIT for three reasons that all bite in this project's
specific situation. It grants patent rights explicitly and terminates them
on patent litigation (§3), which is the clause a commercial store's legal
review looks for before it agrees to redistribute somebody's binary, and
this work is submitted to four of them. It defines NOTICE (§4d), so the
third-party attribution this work package owes has a place inside the
licence instead of being an extra file with no defined standing. And it
requires changed files to be marked (§4b), which matters for a product whose
whole design is redistributing rclone's compiled packages behind a narrow
adapter.
The known cost: Apache-2.0 is incompatible with GPL-2.0-only. That is free
here because the graph has no GPL in it, and permissiveIds is what keeps it
free rather than assumed: an id is admitted by being named, so GPL arriving
through a new dependency is a red build and not a discrepancy nobody looks
for. MPL-2.0 raises no such question, because §3.3 is what permits the
Larger Work to ship under these terms in the first place.

acceptedNonPermissive.scope: File-level weak copyleft. Reciprocity reaches the MPL-covered files themselves and nothing this project writes: a Larger Work combining them with other code may ship under other terms, which is what §3.3 says and what this release does.
acceptedNonPermissive.obligation: MPL-2.0 §3.2(a), read rather than remembered: distributing the covered files in Executable Form obliges this project to make their Source Code Form available as §3.1 describes, AND to inform recipients OF THE EXECUTABLE FORM how to obtain that Source Code Form by reasonable means, in a timely manner, at no more than the cost of distribution. §3.1 adds that recipients must be told the source is governed by the MPL and how to obtain a copy of the licence. §3.2(b) forbids the terms of the executable from limiting or altering their rights in that source, and Apache-2.0 over the Larger Work does not touch them. §3.4 forbids stripping notices out of the covered source, which is moot here because neither module is modified.
rationale: Accepted, not tolerated. The two modules arrive under rclone's s3 backend
through github.com/IBM/go-sdk-core/v5 and backend/s3 imports that with no
build tag, so the backend cannot be registered without them. Not shipping
the backend removes the only non-local storage medium the product has, and
forking rclone to drop ibm_signer.go is a cost on every upgrade.
The discharge is cheap because neither module is modified or vendored: the
immutable module proxy serves the exact source that was compiled, go.sum
pins its hash, and each module ships its own MPL text inside that zip. So
a recipient can fetch the source, check it against the release, and read
the licence, without an account and without this repository being public.
sourceRetrieval renders per component rather than naming a project,
because §3.2 is about the source of what shipped and a link to a moving
branch does not identify that.
components names the exact releases somebody read, and the acceptance
covers those and nothing else. A version bump is a different upload with
its own licence bytes and its own source address, so it is refused until
it is read and added here, by the policy check itself and not only by
the artifacts going stale. The list is checked against the inventory in
both directions, so it cannot hold a release the graph no longer links
either: the bump that removed one is when the offer wants reading again.

visibilityNote: Measured, not assumed: `gh repo view spdrman/rclone-manager --json visibility`
answers PRIVATE today. §73 WP5.2 wants the source, privacy, licence and
support links to resolve to real, current content for a store reviewer, and a
private repository resolves to a 404 for everyone outside the ACL. So every
link whose target is this repository is NOT publicly reachable while this says
private, which is why storeReadyForPublicLinks is derived from this one field
instead of being asserted per link. Flipping it to public is the operator
action that closes the criterion; nothing here can do it, and nothing here
docs/compliance/source-offer.md is the written offer that stands in the
meantime: it is what a reviewer is given when the repository itself cannot be
opened, and it is the artifact Apache-2.0 §4a's redistribution obligation is

note: Every distribution target in conformance.json appears here exactly once, and
TestEveryDistributionTargetIsDeclared pins the two sets together in both
directions. A target with no artifacts and no unbuiltReason is refused: a
checksum manifest over an empty set of artifacts passes by having nothing to
compare, which is the failure mode this whole work package exists to stop.
Every target additionally ships the canonical multi-architecture OCI image.
That is recorded once, in container/release-manifest.json, not repeated per

dockge.unbuiltReason: this target ships no artifact of its own on purpose: Dockge imports container/compose.yaml itself, whose digests the generic target above already records, and a second copy here would hash a file nobody distributes twice

synology.unbuiltReason: the shipped artifact is a .spk, assembled by apps/synology/cmd/spkctl at release time rather than checked in; #85 owns building it and re-deriving each embedded binary's SHA-256 out of the finished package against container/release-manifest.json

ugos.unbuiltReason: the shipped artifact is a .upk, packed by ugcli against a known canonical image digest; that build is EPIC D's #83 and its App Center submission is #178, neither of which happens in this repository's gate

note: #81 asks that the refactor's performance evidence travel with the release
rather than staying in the issues that produced it. The seven metric names
below are pinned as a set so one cannot be dropped quietly; the values are
All seven read pending today, honestly: #165 captures the baselines and
#167/#170 record the after numbers, and none of the three has merged to main.
A pending slot is not a satisfied criterion and this file does not claim it
is - what it buys is that the gap is enumerated and named rather than absent.
